paras: The lynching of Deering was the hanging of a young prisoner named Deering by a mob in western Coryell County, Texas, in February 1882, after he was taken from the officer carrying him to the Gatesville jail. Days later armed men from his home neighborhood rode into Gatesville and demanded the arrest of the lynchers, and the sheriff jailed a man named Leverett and his two sons. That reversal, with the victim's neighbors threatening to take the law into their own hands against a lynch mob, carried the story by wire to papers across the country.

The papers disagree about why Deering was in custody. The St. Louis wire said he was under arrest on suspicion of horse stealing. The Belton Journal, reprinted in the San Saba News, said instead that 'Bullet Deering' had been arrested for carrying a pistol, tried before a magistrate and fined one hundred dollars and costs, and was ordered to the Gatesville jail when he could not pay.

According to the Belton Journal, the officer and his prisoner stopped for the night at the house of Esquire King before reaching Gatesville. During the night, which the paper gave as 'Monday night, the 13th inst.', a mob took charge of Deering, carried him about three hundred yards from the house and hanged him. The wire placed the lynching only 'a few days ago' in 'the western part of the county' and said he was taken 'from an officer'. No account names Deering's race or the number in the mob.

A Gatesville special dated February 24 reported that citizens of Cowhouse, Deering's neighborhood, had come to town the day before to demand the arrest of 'the murderers of young Deering'. The Dallas Weekly Herald put the party at about one hundred, while the Austin Statesman's copy of the same dispatch said about two hundred. The wire described them as armed and quoted their warning that otherwise 'they would take the law into their own hands'.

On an affidavit sworn by members of the party, Justice Hedgepeth issued a warrant, and Sheriff Friend and a posse left that night. They returned about noon on February 24 with Bob Leverett, spelled 'Divenett' in the Austin paper, and his two sons, who were jailed, and other arrests were expected. The Brenham Weekly Banner reported on March 9 that Robert Leverett and his two sons, 'charged with lynching Deering', had a preliminary examination and were put under a nominal bond to appear before the district court. No report of an indictment or district court trial appears in the coverage.

The first national report was a Texas special to the St. Louis Republican, relayed from St. Louis on February 25 and 26 and garbled in transmission to 'Gainesville', 'Galesville', 'Galesburg' and 'Gattsville'. Between February 26 and 28 it ran in St. Paul, Memphis, Savannah, Washington, Wilmington, Portland, Augusta, Eureka and Cheyenne, and a rewritten digest appeared in Lancaster and Wilmington papers and later in the Yorkville Enquirer and the Democratic Advocate. Headlines dwelt on the reprisal rather than the hanging: 'Lynching and Reprisal' in St. Paul, 'Justice Demanded' in Augusta, 'Alleged Lynchers Arrested' in Wilmington and 'Mob Law' in Cheyenne. The Memphis Daily Appeal headed it 'A New Departure', and one Nevada copy said 'the vigilantes' had taken Deering.

Texas papers carried fuller local material. The Austin Statesman titled the Gatesville special 'Citizens Demand Punishment for Mob Violence', and the special itself called the lynchers murderers. The Belton Journal took a different line, writing that it could not think 'the mob hung the man merely for carrying a pistol' and that the mob 'must have had some better excuse'.

The charge against Deering is reported two ways: suspicion of horse stealing in the St. Louis wire, and a pistol-carrying fine he could not pay in the Belton Journal, a nearer Texas source with more procedural detail. The dates also vary: the Belton Journal put the lynching on Monday night the 13th, while an Indiana brief said 'on Saturday', apparently confusing it with the armed men's visit, which the local Gatesville dispatch dates to February 23.

reader.title: Lynching of Deering
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob took Deering from the officer or officers holding him and hanged him (A1, A15, A17).

Every account says a mob took Deering from officers and hanged or 'lynched' him (A1, A15, A17), with a criminal accusation as the pretext, horse stealing in the wire (A1) or carrying a pistol in the Belton Journal (A17). The mob's size is never given, but 'a mob' and the arrest of a father and two sons with others sought (A15, A18) indicate three or more.

The St. Louis wire (A1, A11), a separate Gatesville special (A13, A15) and the Belton Journal (A17) independently agree that a mob took Deering from officers and hanged him, though they differ on the charge against him.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire (St. Louis Republican special)
accounts.gist: A mob in the western part of the county took Deering, under arrest on suspicion of horse stealing, from an officer and lynched him; a hundred armed men from his neighborhood then forced the arrest of Leverett and two sons.

accounts.label: Gatesville special (Dallas Herald, Austin Statesman)
accounts.gist: Cowhouse citizens came to town on Feb. 23 to demand the arrest of 'the murderers of young Deering'; on their affidavit a warrant issued and the sheriff jailed Leverett and two sons on Feb. 24.

accounts.label: Belton Journal (via San Saba News)
accounts.gist: Deering had been fined $100 and costs for carrying a pistol and was being taken to the Gatesville jail when a mob seized him at Esquire King's on Monday night the 13th and hanged him; the editor doubted the pistol charge was the mob's reason.

framing.detail: Papers from Maine to Nevada ran the St. Louis wire under headlines on the reprisal rather than the lynching: 'Lynching and Reprisal', 'Justice Demanded', 'After the Lynchers', 'Alleged Lynchers Arrested'.
The Austin Statesman headed the Gatesville special 'Citizens Demand Punishment for Mob Violence', and the special called the lynchers 'the murderers of young Deering'.
The Belton Journal, reprinted in San Saba, doubted the mob hanged Deering 'merely for carrying a pistol' and supposed it 'must have had some better excuse'.
